description: we’re building groundtruth — a radar-first web tool that uses nisar + sentinel-1 SAR data to visualize how earth’s surface is changing where optical satellites go blind.
summary:
FloodLens makes satellite radar flood data readable by anyone. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) can map floodwater across whole provinces, but a raw radar image is grey speckle that only specialists can interpret, so the people who need the answer rarely see it.

We built a single-page web app that takes one real event, the 2022 Pakistan floods, and places Sentinel-1 radar and NASA Landsat optical imagery of the same ground in one aligned frame, with a swipe comparison, a plain-language explainer and an interactive map.

We then measured it. Over a 22,000 km² scene of Sindh, radar alone mapped about 9,300 km² of water and Landsat about 9,400 km², within 2% of each other. The two maps classify the same ground identically on 76% of pixels, against 51% expected by chance. Two independent sensors, one answer, shown in a form anyone can read.
details:
What it does. FloodLens turns a hard-to-read data type into something anyone can understand.

The problem: satellite radar (SAR) can map floodwater at scale, but raw radar imagery looks like noise to non-specialists. Our solution: for the 2022 Pakistan floods (33 million people affected, 1,700+ deaths), we place real Sentinel-1 radar and Landsat optical imagery of the same ground into one aligned frame. Visitors read a three-part brief (problem, question, finding), drag a swipe control to compare the two views, switch the optical layer between before and during the flood, see the measured results, locate the event on an interactive map, and learn how radar reads water from an animated diagram.

What we found. We asked whether a radar flood map holds up against what the eye can see. Over one 188 x 118 km window of Sindh (22,124 km²), radar alone maps about 9,300 km² of water and Landsat about 9,400 km², within 2%. The two classify the same ground identically on 76% of pixels, against 51% by chance. Landsat shows water coverage more than doubling between 4 and 28 August 2022. These are simple threshold classifiers shown for illustration, not an operational flood product, and the site states each method and how much the numbers move with the thresholds.

How it works. Smooth water reflects radar away from the satellite, so flooded ground appears dark. We used NASA Earth Observatory Landsat 8 and 9 imagery (4 and 28 Aug 2022) and a Sentinel-1A scene from 30 Aug 2022 (terrain-corrected, VV polarisation, via Microsoft Planetary Computer). The Landsat images are tilted about 12 degrees from north, so we solved the rotation and offset by correlating water masks, verified the overlay by eye, and resampled the radar into the Landsat frame. Radar water is backscatter below -13 dB, a threshold chosen from the data (Otsu), not tuned.

Benefits and impact. It makes radar flood data understandable to journalists, educators, students and planners with no GIS background, and shows with a measurable case that radar and optical agree. It is open source, so another event or region is another case study. Every figure comes with its method and uncertainty.

Tools. Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, React Leaflet, react-compare-image, Framer Motion, Lenis; Python (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow) for registration and measurement; Vercel for hosting.

What is creative. Pairing the two sensors in one registered frame, and leading with measured results instead of claims.

Factors we considered. Validity (stated uncertainty, no overclaiming), accessibility for non-specialists, open data and licensing, and no NASA branding.

Code: https://github.com/alisharubab/FloodLens

AI use: Claude Code (Anthropic) was used to help write and review code, the image-analysis scripts and the project text. The team chose the case study, framing and design, and checked the results.
